name: K'iche', Cunén
confidence_why: Henderson 2012 and Barrett 2002, each from their own fieldwork, and the surveys Bennett 2016 and DiCanio & Bennett 2018 all put main stress on the final syllable (the last heavy or root syllable), so the placement is settled; only the alternating secondary stresses in the rule are doubtful, since Barrett 2002 counts them from the left edge and Bennett 2016 treats every report of secondary stress…

new_statements.quote: In K'ichee' roots and stems, word-final CVC and CVV syllables receive primary stress. Secondary stress occurs in words of three or more syllables and falls on the initial syllable and consecutive alternating syllables moving left to right. Secondary stress does not occur on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable (i.e. stress clash between secondary and primary stress is not allowed). [p. 1] ... The phrase-medial cliticized forms demonstrate that the primary stress is actually a moraic trochee aligned at rightmost edge. The feet for secondary stress are syllabic trochees moving left to right. Stress clash and degenerate feet are prohibited [p. 2]
new_statements.citation: Barrett, Rusty. 2002. Mora alignment and multiple foot types in K'ichee'. Linguistics Presentations 3, University of Kentucky UKnowledge (analysis of stress in the Nahualá dialect).
new_statements.locator: sec. 0 and sec. 1 'Stress patterns in K'ichee'', paper pp. 1-2 (PDF pp. 2-3); examples (1)-(3); fn. 1 (data = Nahualá dialect, field notes Barrett 1993)

new_statements.relation_note: Primary placement agrees with the catalog (final). The catalog alternating stress from the right matches Barrett for 2-, 3- and 5-syllable words but NOT for 4-syllable words: Barrett's left-aligned syllabic trochees give 1001 (ètamab'ál 'science', tìkoonijél 'farmer', àwiioqíl 'your wife'), whereas the catalog's 0101 counts alternation from the right (the uncited Wikipedia 'iambic pattern' sentence). Barrett also adds a weight/position condition the catalog lacks: a light word-final syllable (only in phrase-medial cliticized verbs) takes penultimate primary stress. The catalog's existing_statements list is empty, so nothing else to compare; the earlier downloaded Bennett 2016 (p. 497) flags…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress goes on the word-final syllable when it is heavy (CVC or CVV) — which is every root/stem, since these end in a consonant (porór, kajíb', atsíb', tìnamít, ètamab'ál). Weight counts only word-finally ('CVV and CVC syllables in K'ichee' only count as heavy when they are word final', p. 3). When a phrase-medial cliticized verb form ends in a light CV syllable (clitic final C lost), primary stress falls on the penult (imb'éb'i, kimb'éti; glottal-final clitics lengthen and keep final stress: ìmb'ewíi, kìmb'enalóo). Formally: a moraic trochee at the right edge (final mora alignment) plus left-to-right syllabic trochees for secondary stress, no clash, no degenerate feet (ranking in (10), p. 4).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: in words of 3+ syllables, on the initial syllable and alternating syllables left-to-right, quantity-insensitive (tìkoonijél, àwiioqíl, kàtikrìkiník, kàtoqtòqiník, xìnts'ib'àapaník, p. 2); never adjacent to the primary (no clash), so 3-syl = 101 (tìnamít, k'òlok'ík), 4-syl = 1001 (ètamab'ál, tìkoonijél), 5-syl = 10101 (kàtoqtòqiník, kàwunùnwutík). Note the paper's own prose ('does not occur on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable') is contradicted by its 5-syllable data and tableau (4), where secondary stress sits on the antepenult; the tableau/data pattern (syllabic trochees L-to-R, *CLASH) is the analysis actually argued.
new_statements.exceptions: Cliticized verb forms adjacent to a clause boundary keep final stress; phrase-medial cliticized forms with a light final syllable shift primary stress to the penult (sec. 1, ex. (3), p. 2). Data are from one dialect (Nahualá) and one consultant (Gregorio Tum), impressionistic field notes.
new_statements.identity_note: Barrett 2002 describes the Nahualá dialect of K'ichee' (fn. 1: field notes, consultant Gregorio Tum), not Cunén. kich1264 'K'iche', Cunén' is a retired-ISO bookkeeping code identity-mapped to K'iche' (kich1262); no work opened or listed says anything Cunén-specific. Baird 2014 (unopened) is on K'ichee' generally per its title.

readall_conflicts: Only Barrett 2002 could be opened. Within it, primary stress is final for all roots and stems (every root/stem ends in a heavy CVC/CVV syllable), shifting to the penult only when a phrase-medial clitic leaves a light final syllable — i.e. final-if-heavy-else-penult, restricted to a final two-syllable window (what Bennett 2016 fn. 22 calls 'weight-conditioned penultimate stress' and what Henderson 2012's held generalization phrases as 'unless that syllable is light non-root material'). That is compatible with the catalog's final primary. The disagreement is over secondary stress: Barrett's left-to-right syllabic trochees give 1001 for 4-syllable words, against the catalog's 0101; and Barrett's own prose ('not on the penultimate or antepenultimate') is inconsistent with his 5-syllable data (kàtoqtòqiník, secondary on the antepenult). Independently, the already-held Bennett 2016 (p. 497) and DiCanio & Bennett 2018 say most Mayan languages lack rhythmic secondary stress and that reports like Barrett 2002 are impressionistic; the catalog's secondaries rest on an uncited Wikipedia sentence plus Barrett's Nahualá field notes. Baird 2014, the one instrumental study, remains unread (academia.edu 403; MITWPL print-only).
